symptoms: Holes in leaves and flowers Larvae boring into fruits or pods Premature fruit or flower drop Damaged cotton bolls producing poor quality lint Presence of frass and feeding tunnels in fruits or grains
description: Helicoverpa armigera, known as the cotton bollworm, is a highly polyphagous moth pest distributed across Africa, Europe, Asia, Australia, and South America. The larval stage feeds on leaves, buds, flowers, fruits, and seeds of many crops, causing severe economic losses. Adults are capable of long-distance migration, allowing rapid spread and multiple generations per year in warm climates.
management: monitoring: Regular scouting for eggs, larvae, and feeding damage Use pheromone traps to monitor adult populations Light traps can also help detect moth activity cultural_control: Crop rotation with non-host crops Removal of crop residues and weeds Deep ploughing after harvest to destroy pupae Use of trap crops such as sunflower or marigold mechanical_control: Handpicking and destroying larvae and eggs Using traps and physical barriers Removal of infested fruits or plant parts biological_control: microorganisms: Helicoverpa nucleopolyhedrovirus (HaNPV) Baculovirus species targeting lepidopteran larvae Isaria fumosorosea (entomopathogenic fungus) macroorganisms: Trichogramma pretiosum (egg parasitoid wasp) Habrobracon hebetor (larval parasitoid) chemical_control: note: Chemical control should be used as part of Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and only when pest populations exceed economic thresholds. active_ingredients: Spinosad Emamectin benzoate Indoxacarb Lambda-cyhalothrin Chlorantraniliprole genetic_control: Cultivation of Bt cotton expressing Bacillus thuringiensis toxins (Cry1Ab, Cry1Ac, Cry2Ab, Vip3A)
